Strategy for Localizing an Adaptive-Learning Platform Across Vietnam, Saudi Arabia, France, and Kenya

## Executive recommendation

The platform should ship as a **single, configurable core wrapped in country "pods"** that own curriculum, language, pedagogy, content moderation, distribution, and compliance. The four markets differ on three axes—**regulation of what is taught (curriculum authority)**, **who pays (parents vs. ministries vs. schools)**, and **how learning is socially framed (screen-time, testing, religion, laïcité)**—so the right abstraction is not "one product with translations" but **a platform whose content, assessment, and channel layers are pluggable**, while the AI engine, learning science backbone, content authoring, analytics, and trust infrastructure stay shared.

Three operating principles should govern every decision:

1. **Content and curriculum are configuration, not code.** If localizing Vietnam requires an engineer to ship, the architecture is wrong.
2. **Trust is a feature, not a checklist.** Data residency, content review, pedagogical credibility, and government accreditation are first-class product surfaces, especially in France and Saudi Arabia.
3. **Each market needs a dedicated pod with global guardrails.** Country teams own curriculum accuracy, language quality, channel packaging, and teacher/parent UX; the global core owns the learning engine, security model, analytics, and platform reliability.

A "one global product" posture will fail in France (parents reject generic pedagogy and demand data sovereignty) and in Saudi Arabia (no MoE tender without local content moderation and Arabic-native assessment norms). A "four separate products" posture will bankrupt unit economics. The right answer sits between the two.

---

## 1. What is shared, what is local

### 1.1 Shared global core (one engineering team, one codebase)

| Layer | What it does | Why it stays global |
|---|---|---|
| Adaptive learning engine | Models learner knowledge, recommends next item, calibrates difficulty | Learning-science R&D is the company's IP; replicating per country destroys the moat |
| Authoring & content CMS | Lets curriculum teams author, version, tag, and A/B test items | A single source of truth avoids "Vietnam 2024 vs. Vietnam 2025" drift |
| Assessment & item-bank primitives | IRT/CAT engines, psychometrics, equating | Psychometric validity is the hardest thing to redo |
| Analytics & data warehouse | Learning telemetry, dashboards, outcomes measurement | Outcomes evidence feeds every sales conversation in every country |
| Identity, auth, payments plumbing | SSO, parent accounts, school rosters, billing | Engineering scale and security discipline |
| Safety & trust stack | Content moderation APIs, PII handling, audit logs | A breach in one market becomes a regulatory problem in all |
| AI policy & guardrails | Tutor persona, refusal behavior, hallucination control | Brand consistency; avoids divergent AI behavior across borders |

### 1.2 Country pod (local team, local accountability)

| Pod layer | What it owns | Examples across the four markets |
|---|---|---|
| Curriculum pack | Standards mapping, item coverage, scaffolding | Vietnam MoET 2018; France "Programmes officiels" cycle 2/3/4; KICD CBC; Saudi MoE + Tatweer |
| Language & cultural adaptation | Translation, voice, examples, names, holidays | Arabic (MSA + dialect flagging), French (Académie standards), Vietnamese (diacritics, north/center/south variants), English + Swahili + mother-tongue hooks in Kenya |
| Pedagogical wrapper | Pacing, screen-time budget, teacher-led mode, parent reporting cadence | France: teacher-mediated, ≤20-min sessions; Kenya: mobile bursts, USSD parent reports; Saudi: gender-aware UX, Islamic-studies integration |
| Distribution packaging | App store presence, school rostering, MoE integrations, telco bundles | B2C app in Vietnam; MoE API in Saudi; ENT (Environnement Numérique de Travail) integrations in France; Safaricom/Airtel bundles in Kenya |
| Compliance & accreditation | Data residency, content review boards, regulator filings | EU AI Act + CNIL in France; NCA/CST/SDAIA in Saudi; KICD approval + county MoUs in Kenya; MoET accreditation in Vietnam |
| Commercial model | Pricing, channel, partner economics | Consumer freemium (Vietnam, France); MoE tenders (Saudi); county PPPs (Kenya); hybrid (France schools) |

The **clean abstraction is a curriculum adapter**: an interface that turns a national standards document into (a) the item tags the engine expects, (b) the assessment blueprint (formative, summative, high-stakes), and (c) the reporting shape regulators and parents want to see. Once this adapter is well designed, adding a fifth country is a content project, not an engineering project.

---

## 2. Country playbooks

The four markets fall into four archetypes that should guide sequencing and staffing:

| Dimension | Vietnam | Saudi Arabia | France | Kenya |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Curriculum authority | MoET, mandated, top-down | MoE + Tatweer, mandated, centralized | Ministry, very prescriptive (cycles, compétences) | KICD, CBC, competency-based, evolving |
| Language | Vietnamese (diacritics) | Arabic (RTL, MSA) | French (Académie, laïcité) | English + Swahili + mother tongue (Grades 1–3) |
| Parental attitude | High investment, anxious about English/math, growing screen-time concern | Strong value on education, religious/cultural content scrutiny, gender norms | Skeptical of screens, demands pedagogical credibility, GDPR-aware | Pragmatic, outcomes-oriented, mobile-first, cost-sensitive |
| Dominant channel | B2C parents (tutoring market); growing B2G/school | B2G (large MoE tenders); premium private | B2C supplementary + schools (mairies, académies) + publishers | B2G (national + 47 counties); NGOs/World Bank; telco bundles |
| Trust signals that matter | MoET accreditation, Vietnamese data, teacher endorsements | Local content moderation, MoE approval, Arabic-native assessment, gender/religious compliance | CNIL, EU AI Act, French pedagogy experts, publisher partnerships | KICD approval, county MoUs, low-bandwidth proof, Swahili quality |
| Entry archetype | Consumer-first, school add-on | Government-first, premium consumer optional | Publisher/school-first, consumer optional | Government + NGO-led pilots, scale via county contracts |

### 2.1 Vietnam — consumer-led with school credibility

The tutoring market is enormous and parent-funded, but MoET alignment is non-negotiable: schools will not recommend a tool that does not map to the 2018 curriculum, and parents will not trust one that does not reflect what is on the test. The product should ship as a **parent-facing B2C subscription** with a **teacher dashboard add-on** for after-school programs. Three localizations matter beyond translation: (a) diacritics and northern/central/southern variants in voice and examples, (b) explicit MoET standards mapping surfaced to parents ("covers 70% of Grade 5 math curriculum"), and (c) a screen-time-aware "focus mode" with printable worksheets and parent-defined session caps to neutralize the screen-time objection. English-language proficiency is the highest-value premium upsell. Distribution should lean on KOL teachers on TikTok and Facebook, with school pilots via education publishers for B2B2C credibility. Government tenders exist but are slower and more price-sensitive; treat them as a 12–24 month build, not a launch dependency.

### 2.2 Saudi Arabia — government-led with cultural compliance

The Ministry of Education and Tatweer (now part of the Human Capability Endowments) drive most large EdTech spend, and Vision 2030 has created explicit appetite for AI-in-education. A B2G-led entry is the only viable scale path; a consumer-only entry will hit an Arabic content moderation ceiling within weeks. The product should ship with (a) **Arabic-native assessment norms**, not translated English ones (psychometric differences, especially in early literacy, are real), (b) a **content review board** including Islamic-studies and Arabic-language experts, (c) **gender-aware UX** that respects school segregation norms without making them awkward, and (d) **Vision 2030 alignment** in the tender narrative (human capital, future skills, Arabic-language AI). Data residency (in-region or on-prem for MoE deployments), local entity presence, and Arabic-speaking customer success are prerequisites, not nice-to-haves. Premium private schools and a household consumer SKU can follow once MoE credibility is established.

### 2.3 France — pedagogical-credibility-led with EU compliance

French parents and teachers are not anti-technology; they are **anti-generic-technology**. The product must be positioned as a *outil pédagogique* designed *par* and *avec* desenseignants français, not an American AI tutor translated into French. Three non-negotiables: (a) **EU AI Act compliance** (high-risk educational AI classification likely), with a published risk management file, model card, and human-in-the-loop for consequential decisions; (b) **CNIL-grade data protection**, with EU data residency, minimal data collection, and DPIA-ready documentation; (c) **pedagogical credibility**, achieved by hiring a French chief pedagogical officer, partnering with a recognized French publisher (e.g., Hatier, Nathan, Belin) for content co-authorship, and aligning to the *programmes officiels* by cycle and compétence. Screen-time concerns are real and should be answered by design: default to teacher-mediated sessions under 20 minutes, surface "compétences travaillées" reporting, and offer printable/onenote integrations. Distribution is hybrid: consumer freemium for parents who want après-la-classe reinforcement, school licensing via académies and mairies, and publisher bundles for retail. Government procurement (Ministère, collectivités) is slow but high-value and should be pursued as a parallel track once school references exist.

### 2.4 Kenya — government + telco + NGO ecosystem

Kenya's CBC is the most permissive of the four curricula (competency-based, teacher judgment matters, less item-bank rigidity), but the go-to-market is the hardest: national MoE is slow, **47 semi-autonomous counties** drive most school spend, telcos (Safaricom, Airtel) control distribution, and World Bank/UNICEF/NGO funding shapes pilots. The product must be **mobile-first and low-bandwidth** from day one: an Android app under 30 MB, offline content packs, USSD or SMS for parent reports, and M-Pesa/Airtel Money billing. Language strategy is layered: English and Swahili as the spine, with hooks for mother-tongue early-grade support (Kikuyu, Luo, Kalenjin, etc.) where CBC explicitly requires it. The right entry is a **county pilot** (e.g., one of the CBC early-adopter counties) co-designed with KICD, evaluated by a credible local university, and co-funded by an NGO or development financier. Once outcomes are published, scale horizontally to other counties and vertically within the same county. Consumer subscriptions are a secondary channel and will likely need to be priced at a level most households can afford (under USD 2/month).

---

## 3. The shared core, designed for localization

### 3.1 Curriculum as a first-class data model

The most consequential architectural decision is treating national curricula as **versioned, machine-readable data**, not embedded in application logic. The data model should express:

- **Strand/topic/competency** hierarchy with stable IDs across countries where possible (e.g., "compare fractions" maps cleanly across curricula).
- **Proficiency scales** (binary mastery, rubric levels, performance bands) because different systems express "good" differently.
- **Assessment blueprints** (formative vs. summative, high-stakes vs. low-stakes, teacher-judged vs. machine-scored).
- **Content coverage reports** that show, per curriculum, what percentage is authored, reviewed, and QA-passed.

This lets the same engine serve a French parent who wants to see "compétence 3 — lire et comprendre un texte littéraire" and a Saudi MoE official who wants to see "تغطية المعايير — الصف الرابع الابتدائي" against the same underlying learner state.

### 3.2 Localization beyond translation

Three layers that are routinely conflated and should not be:

1. **Linguistic localization**: translation, voice, diacritics, RTL, date/number formats, names, examples. A standard i18n/L10n pipeline, ideally with in-country human review for every content release.
2. **Cultural localization**: illustrations, colors, names, holidays, food, family structures, religious references. Saudi and France require explicit content moderation boards; Vietnam and Kenya require cultural consultants, not just translators.
3. **Pedagogical localization**: pacing, scaffolding, teacher vs. learner agency, error-handling tone, parent reporting, assessment philosophy. France demands a Socratic, teacher-mediated approach; Kenya's CBC demands open-ended, project-based tasks; Vietnam's high-stakes culture demands test-prep fluency; Saudi's Islamic-studies integration demands explicit values alignment.

A common failure mode is to invest in (1), do a little of (2), and skip (3) entirely. In France and Saudi this failure is fatal.

### 3.3 Trust infrastructure as a product

A single global trust stack should expose, per country:

- Data residency controls (EU-only, Saudi-only, etc.) enforceable at the row level in the warehouse.
- A content moderation API with country-specific policy packs (e.g., a stricter pack for Saudi covering religious content; a laïcité pack for France covering religious imagery in public-sector deployments).
- Model cards and DPIAs per country, generated from a single source.
- Audit logs that satisfy NCA, CNIL, KICD, and MoET review processes simultaneously.

Building this once and configuring it per country is materially cheaper than retrofitting it after a regulator complaint.

---

## 4. Distribution: three channels, four go-to-markets

The platform should support three commercial channels, deployed differently per country:

| Channel | Best fit | Key mechanics |
|---|---|---|
| **B2C consumer** | Vietnam (primary), France (secondary) | App store, freemium, parent subscriptions, viral hooks |
| **B2B school** | France (primary), Vietnam (secondary) | Per-seat licensing, rostering, teacher dashboards, publisher bundles |
| **B2G procurement** | Saudi (primary), Kenya (primary), France (tertiary) | Tender response, outcomes contracts, county/national pilots, accreditation |

### 4.1 Channel-specific product surfaces

- **Consumer SKU**: parent app, child profile, weekly report, screen-time controls, freemium → premium conversion.
- **School SKU**: roster sync, teacher dashboard, class assignments, gradebook, parent-teacher communication, school admin reporting.
- **Government SKU**: district/ministry dashboard, equity reporting (gender, region, disability), offline deployment kits, on-prem option, multi-year outcomes contracts.

Each SKU should be a **packaging of the same engine**, not a separate codebase. The risk to manage is that B2G requirements (on-prem, custom SSO, equity reports) start consuming engineering attention disproportionately; ring-fence a government engineering team and charge for custom work.

### 4.2 Partner ecosystem

- **France**: publishers (Hatier, Nathan, Belin, Magnard), CNED for distance learning alignment, académies, French AI research labs (INRIA) for credibility.
- **Saudi**: Tatweer-aligned local systems integrators, Arabic content houses, Islamic-studies review bodies, gender-segregated school networks.
- **Kenya**: KICD, county governments, Safaricom/Airtel, World Bank/UNICEF/Gates Foundation, local universities for evaluation.
- **Vietnam**: MoET-accredited publishers, KOL teachers, Vietnamese AI research labs, telcos (Viettel, Mobifone) for distribution.

A partner-led distribution is faster and cheaper than direct sales in all four markets; the global team should provide a **partner enablement kit** (sales decks, technical integration docs, certification paths) rather than a direct sales force everywhere.

---

## 5. Pricing and commercial design

Pricing models should differ by channel and country, but a few principles apply:

- **Outcomes-based pricing for B2G**: per-learner-per-month with a learning-gains overlay in Saudi and Kenya; risk-share on measured improvement, not seat counts alone.
- **Per-seat school pricing in France**: aligned to French public-procurement norms; multi-year framework agreements with académies.
- **Consumer freemium in Vietnam and France**: free tier covers MoET/French curriculum basics, premium adds adaptive depth, English, and parent reports.
- **Affordable tiers in Kenya**: under USD 2/month consumer; NGO/government-subsidized free tiers for low-income schools; telco bundles for distribution.

Contract length should be **3–5 years for government** (matching ministry planning cycles) and **monthly/annual for consumer**. Avoid multi-year consumer commitments; they create churn and badwill.

---

## 6. Phased roadmap

| Phase | Timeline | Focus | Exit criteria |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0 — Foundation** | Months 0–6 | Build curriculum adapter; stand up four country pods; sign 1 strategic partner per market; complete EU AI Act and Saudi NCA readiness assessments | Architecture review passed; partner MoUs signed; accreditation pathways mapped |
| **1 — First light** | Months 6–18 | Ship Vietnam B2C and one Kenya county pilot in parallel; pursue first Saudi MoE pre-qualification; sign French publisher | 50k MAU Vietnam; Kenya pilot with measured learning gain; Saudi pre-qualified; French publisher deal signed |
| **2 — Scale** | Months 18–36 | Launch France school SKU; convert Kenya pilot to multi-county contract; bid Saudi MoE tender; expand Vietnam to B2B | 4-country revenue >50% of total; B2G contracts in 2 countries; learning-gains evidence published in 3 countries |
| **3 — Consolidate** | Months 36+ | Platform monetization (tutor marketplace, assessment API); fifth-country playbook; outcome-bond financing | Platform GMV growing; one outcome-bond issued; ready to expand to additional French-speaking African, GCC, or ASEAN markets |

Phase 0 is the highest-risk phase: if the curriculum adapter and country pods are not credible by month 6, every later milestone slips. Resist the temptation to ship a single English product first; the retrofit cost will exceed the build cost.

---

## 7. Governance and metrics

### 7.1 Operating model

- **Global product/engineering** owns the core, the curriculum adapter contract, the trust stack, and platform reliability.
- **Country GMs** own P&L, curriculum accuracy, channel execution, and regulatory relationships. They are full-stack leaders, not sales leads.
- **Pedagogical council** (one per country + one global chair) signs off on content releases and AI tutor behavior in their language and culture.
- **Weekly country standups, monthly global review, quarterly board-level portfolio review.**

### 7.2 Shared vs. local KPIs

| Metric | Global | Country-specific |
|---|---|---|
| Engagement (DAU/MAU, session length) | Yes | Yes, benchmarked |
| Learning gain (pre/post, item-bank independent) | Yes | Yes, by curriculum |
| Curriculum coverage % | — | Yes (mandatory) |
| Trust: data incidents, moderation errors | Yes | Yes, by regulator |
| B2G pipeline value, time-to-award | — | Yes (Saudi, Kenya) |
| Consumer LTV/CAC, churn | Yes | Yes |
| Partner-originated revenue % | — | Yes |

A useful guardrail: **no more than 30% of engineering capacity** should be allocated to country-specific customization. If it exceeds that, the abstraction has failed and the platform must be re-architected, not the country team expanded.

### 7.3 Risks to monitor explicitly

- **Curriculum drift**: Vietnam 2018 → 2026 revision; France's evolving AI-in-education guidance; Kenya CBC revisions. Treat curriculum changes as release-train events, not surprises.
- **AI regulatory divergence**: EU AI Act vs. Saudi NCA vs. emerging Vietnamese frameworks. A single global AI policy with country overlays is the only sustainable posture.
- **Content moderation asymmetry**: a moderation incident in one market can become a global PR problem; centralize learning but localize the policy pack.
- **Partner concentration**: relying on one French publisher or one Saudi SI creates key-person risk; keep at least two partner paths alive per market.
- **Country-team talent risk**: four pods require strong local leadership; underinvesting here is the most common cause of stalled international expansions.

---

## 8. What to decide now

The board should approve five things to unlock Phase 0:

1. **Architecture investment** for the curriculum adapter and trust stack, sized for five countries not four.
2. **Four country GM hires** with full P&L authority and local entity setup where required (Saudi is non-negotiable; Kenya optional but helpful for tenders).
3. **A 24-month budget** for Phase 0 and Phase 1, with explicit ring-fenced amounts per pod and a global overhead cap.
4. **A partner strategy** including one publisher (France), one MoE/Tatweer-aligned SI (Saudi), one telco (Kenya), and one Vietnamese publisher or KOL network.
5. **An outcomes measurement framework** that produces publishable learning-gain evidence by month 18, because every later sale depends on it.

If those five decisions are taken, the platform can credibly be in four markets within 18 months with a single core, four pods, and a unit-economics profile that improves as each new country is added. If any one of them is deferred, the company will end up shipping four products, burning cash, and learning the lesson at three times the cost.
